title: Glad three times
hook: glad before giving, glad while giving, glad after (AN 6.37)
carry: glad before, bright during, happy after

segments.voice: Yesterday, pindapata, the alms round: saffron robes at dawn, rice falling into open bowls. Your line was the bowl is open.

You know the kind of gift that goes wrong in the middle. You pick out a present, happy. Then you see the price tag and wince. You wrap it, and a little voice says they'd better appreciate this. A week later you're still annoyed they never mentioned it. The gift has cost you three times: in money, in mood, and in resentment. The Buddha once praised a gift given by a laywoman, and he described exactly what made it shine. Part of his answer was about the giver's heart, and it has three moments.
screen: `HAPPY, THEN THE PRICE TAG.` → `THEY'D BETTER APPRECIATE THIS.` → `THREE MOMENTS OF A GIFT.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Numerical Discourses, book of sixes. A laywoman named Nandamata, known for her devotion, had prepared a gift of food for the community of monks, with the Buddha's two chief disciples, Sariputta and Moggallana, at its head. The Buddha, the text says, saw the offering from afar and told the monks that this gift had six factors. Three belong to the ones who receive: they are free of greed, hatred and delusion, or practicing to be. And three belong to the giver. Before giving, the giver is glad. While giving, the giver's heart is bright and confident. After giving, the giver is uplifted. There's a short Pali verse that people still chant about it: glad before, bright during, happy after. The striking part is that the gladness isn't a reward that comes later. It's part of the gift itself. A gift given grudgingly, with a wince in the middle and resentment after, is still a gift, but it's thinner. A gift given gladly all the way through, the text says, is great in fruit, beyond measuring. So the practice isn't just give more. It's paying attention to how you give: the gladness while you choose it and picture their face, the brightness in the moment of giving, and afterward, instead of waiting for thanks, going back to enjoy it. Recollecting your own generosity is itself a traditional meditation. You're allowed to feel good about a good thing.
screen: `NANDAMATA'S GIFT OF FOOD.` · `THREE FOR THE RECEIVERS.` · `GLAD BEFORE, BRIGHT DURING, HAPPY AFTER.` · `THE GLADNESS IS PART OF THE GIFT.` · then, large: `GLAD THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a gift you gave that went well: a meal, a favor, a present, an hour of help. Remember the gladness of choosing it, the brightness as it reached their hands and face, and how it felt later that day. Let that gladness spread through the body with the breath; nothing to prove, just a good thing you did.
Sumana. Glad-minded, of good heart: the giver's part of a great gift, glad before giving, bright while giving, uplifted after.
Your line: glad before, bright during, happy after. The gladness is part of the gift. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists give with attention to their own state of mind, and recollecting one's past generosity (caganussati) is a traditional meditation; the verse on being glad before, during and after is still chanted.

fork.setup: you gave a friend a thoughtful gift a week ago and they never mentioned it. you notice resentment creeping in. what does this teaching point to?
options: remind them, so they say thank you.
go back and enjoy the gladness of having given.
fork.reveal: the giver's third moment is uplift after giving. it doesn't depend on thanks: you can recollect the gift and be glad.

original.note: Pali: glad-minded, of good heart; the giver is sumana before giving.

trapdoor: what you thought: give generously and don't think about it.
what it means: pay attention to how you give; gladness before, during and after is part of the gift.
what a scholar hears: AN 6.37 gives a six-factored gift, three factors in the donor and three in the recipients; the donor's are often remembered as sumana, pasanna, attamana.
recall: a string of beads that counts recitations

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.37 (Chalangadana Sutta), the six-factored gift

notes: Story details of AN 6.37 (Velukantaki Nandamata's offering to the sangha headed by Sariputta and Moggallana; the Buddha seeing it with the divine eye) are paraphrased; confirm.
The donor's three factors (pubbeva dana sumano, dadam cittam pasadeti, datva attamano) are summarized as glad, bright/confident, uplifted; confirm.
The claim that the verse is 'still chanted' is general; a Keeper may want to specify or soften.
Recollection of generosity is cited to AN 6.10 among the six recollections; confirm.
